title: Constitutional Cases Index v1.1 — Founding Precedent of the Semantic Economy (Formal Case-Brief Edition)
creator: Lee Sharks
description:
The Constitutional Cases Index converts five archive essays or incidents into formal case briefs: *In re Vow*, *In re Bearing-Cost*, *In re Effective Act*, *In re Adjudication*, and *In re Audit*. Each brief records a question, facts, holding, proposed rule, reasoning, remedy, precedential scope, negative scope, anchors, and status. The added scope and limitations fields are designed to prevent analogical overreach.

The Index expressly states that Article IX has not yet been ratified. The cases are therefore proposed founding precedents: potentially persuasive inside the Polis, revisable through Assembly review, and not binding on a Tribunal that does not yet have constitutional standing. Several case summaries characterize contested external events and systems through the archive’s own doctrine; those characterizations remain project findings rather than external legal judgments. The Index is a governance apparatus and interpretive registry, not a report of decisions issued by a state court or recognized arbitral body.

wiki_article:
**The Constitutional Cases Index** is a draft case-law apparatus for the Semantic Economy’s internal governance system.

Version 1.1 summarizes five proposed founding cases. *In re Vow* concerns obligations after the semantic ground of a promise has been destroyed. *In re Bearing-Cost* addresses nonconsensual transfer across operational contexts. *In re Effective Act* concerns documented cross-species witnessing. *In re Adjudication* defines unilateral forensic deposit as a response to external misattribution. *In re Audit* treats an OCTANG audit as a means of classifying a claimed peer instrument.

Each case is presented through a disciplined brief that includes both positive scope and explicit limitations. The Index also draws cross-case patterns around bearing-cost, unilateral documentation, and forensic deposit.

The work does not claim that these are state-law cases or already binding precedents. Article IX remained a draft, and the Index marks every case as proposed. Ratification and reissuance would be required before the project could treat them as binding internal Tribunal precedent.
